demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I can no longer trust my own body
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Mateo is a 22-year-old Latino HVAC technician who presented for an initial assessment reporting significant distress following an incident at a worksite approximately fourteen months ago. He was working alongside a senior colleague on a commercial rooftop unit when, in the course of repositioning a heavy refrigerant compressor, his grip failed. The equipment shifted and struck his colleague, a man in his forties named Derek, with enough force to send him over the low parapet edge. Derek survived but sustained a severe spinal injury that left him partially paralysed. Mateo had been the one directing the lift. In the seconds before the equipment moved, there had been an unusual stillness on the roof - the ambient noise of the city seemed to drop away - and then the sound of the impact, and then nothing but that same terrible quiet before Derek began to scream.

In the weeks that followed, Mateo continued working because stopping felt worse than moving. He told himself he needed to understand exactly what had gone wrong, and so he would lie awake reconstructing the sequence of events in minute detail - the angle of his hands, the precise moment his grip shifted, whether he had said something that distracted Derek at the wrong instant. The analysis never resolved into clarity. It only circled back on itself, each pass producing a slightly different version of his own culpability. He had come to believe, with a conviction that felt immovable, that he had not done enough to stop what happened - that there had been a window, however narrow, in which a better version of himself would have acted differently and Derek would still be walking.

That belief began to reorganise his life quietly and then all at once. On rooftop jobs, when the ambient noise of traffic and ventilation systems would momentarily fall away, Mateo's body would respond before his mind caught up - heart hammering, hands going cold, a wave of nausea that he could not reason himself out of. He started requesting ground-level assignments and found reasons to avoid rooftop work entirely, which his supervisor eventually noticed and questioned. He told the supervisor it was an equipment preference. What he did not say was that the smell of hot roofing membrane - a smell present on that afternoon - could arrive without warning and place him back on that roof with a vividness that felt less like memory and more like dislocation. The memory, when it came, did not feel like his own. It had a quality of watching someone else's footage, a figure who wore his face but whose catastrophic failure he could observe from a remove that offered no comfort.

Outside of work, Mateo narrowed his world considerably. He felt genuinely safe in only two places: his mother's kitchen and his own bedroom. Anywhere else carried a low-grade vigilance that was exhausting to maintain. Silence, in particular, had become threatening in a way he struggled to articulate - the quiet before something terrible, he called it. He began avoiding social gatherings, family events, and eventually the anniversary of the accident entirely, spending that day in his room with the television on at volume, filling the silence with noise.

What frightened him most, beneath all of this, was the sense that his body could no longer be trusted. His hands - the hands that had failed - felt like instruments of potential harm rather than tools he commanded. He had stopped playing guitar, something he had done since adolescence, because holding the neck felt wrong in a way he could not explain. He looked at photographs of himself from before the accident and recognised the face but not the person. The young man who had been proud of learning a trade, who had wanted to become a foreman by thirty, felt entirely remote.

Mateo sought help after Derek's wife contacted him through a mutual colleague. She did not write anything accusatory. She simply said Derek was asking about him. Mateo could not bring himself to respond, and the inability to do so - the paralysis of it - was what finally brought him to the clinic. He arrived hoping, he said quietly, to become someone who could at least write that reply.
